opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a pretty natural and, in many ways, healthy reaction. If you come from traditional robotics, you were trained in a culture that values understanding the system: you write down the dynamics, you think about stability, you reason about why a controller works and when it will fail. So when machine learning comes in and people show a policy that does something impressive but nobody can quite explain why, there's a reflexive skepticism. And some of that skepticism is well founded. A lot of early learning results were brittle, they worked in one lab on one setup, and they didn't transfer.

But I'd say the response has gone through a few stages. At first there was some dismissal: "this is just curve fitting, it won't generalize, real robots need guarantees." Then, as results got better, especially in manipulation, where modeling contact and deformable objects is genuinely hard, people started to recognize that some problems just aren't tractable with hand-written models. You can't write down the physics of folding a shirt or cooking in a messy kitchen precisely enough to plan over it. That's where data really shines.

And now I think many traditional roboticists are actually becoming some of the most valuable people in the learning era, because they understand hardware, they understand what makes data good, they understand failure modes. The best systems I've seen combine both: learning handles the parts that are hard to model, and classical structure, things like control at the low level, safety constraints, good state estimation, keeps the whole thing reliable.

So my honest view is that it's less a fight between two camps and more a merging. The traditional people bring rigor and an intuition for the physical world; the learning people bring scalability and generality. The friction is real, but it's productive friction. Personally, I think anyone working in robotics today benefits from respecting both: being humble about what our models can capture, and equally humble about what data alone can do.

r001.rationale: It says that as machine-learning results improved, traditional roboticists began to recognize that learning can help with problems that are difficult to model.

r002.rationale: It says traditional roboticists understand hardware, but does not attribute that expertise to extensive experience modifying or refining hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to start by understanding where traditional roboticists came from. For decades, robotics was fundamentally about control theory, kinematics, dynamics, motion planning. These are very mathematically rigorous disciplines. You derive the equations of your system, you prove stability, you know exactly why your controller does what it does. There is a kind of intellectual beauty to it, and also a very real engineering culture around it: if a robot arm in a factory fails, somebody can trace back exactly which assumption broke.

So when machine learning, and especially deep learning, started showing up in robotics around the mid-2010s, the first reaction from a lot of people was skepticism, and honestly some of it was well deserved. Early learning results were often demonstrated in very narrow settings, on a single robot, with a single task, and they would break the moment you changed the lighting or moved the camera. Traditional researchers looked at that and said, this is not robotics, this is a demo. And they had a point. Many of us in the learning community were a bit naive about how hard the real world is.

But I think the response has evolved through a few stages. The first was dismissal. The second was something like a cultural divide, where you had learning people and classical people at the same conferences almost speaking different languages. One side cared about sample efficiency and generalization, the other cared about guarantees and interpretability. There was friction over what counts as a contribution.

Then the third stage, which I think we are in now, is a kind of pragmatic convergence. The classical researchers who were most thoughtful did not reject learning. They asked a much sharper question: where does learning actually belong in the stack? And it turns out the answer is quite interesting. Perception is one place where learning clearly won. Nobody writes hand-coded feature detectors anymore. High-level decision making and manipulation in unstructured environments is another, because the variability is simply too large to model by hand. But low-level control, safety constraints, things where you need a guarantee, the classical tools are still extremely valuable, and the best systems combine the two.

I would also say the traditional community has influenced the learning community more than people acknowledge. The emphasis on real-world evaluation, on robustness, on asking what happens when the model is wrong, those came from them. They kept us honest.

So if I had to summarize, I would say the response started defensive, went through a period of genuine tension, and is now settling into something healthier, where the question is less about which camp is right and more about which tool fits which problem. The people I admire most are the ones who can move fluidly between both worlds, because that is really what the field needs right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from skepticism to pragmatic convergence and points to areas where learning has clearly succeeded, such as perception and unstructured manipulation.

r002.rationale: It mentions diagnosing a factory robot arm failure, but does not attribute traditional researchers’ expertise to extensive experience modifying and refining hardware.

astra-6.text:
I think the response is mixed, and that’s understandable. Traditional robotics researchers have spent years working on control, planning, and understanding physical systems. So when machine learning starts producing impressive results, they naturally ask: How reliable is it? What happens outside the training distribution? Can we explain why it works, or predict when it will fail? Those are important questions when a robot is acting in the physical world.

There may also be some discomfort as the tools and skills that the field values change. But I wouldn’t interpret all skepticism as resistance to progress. A successful demonstration and a dependable robot are different things.

To me, the productive direction is to bring those perspectives together. Learning can help us handle things that are difficult to model explicitly, while traditional robotics gives us ways to reason about constraints, stability, and safety. The interesting question is where each approach helps us build a more capable, reliable system.

r001.rationale: The response mentions impressive machine-learning results, but does not say those demonstrations may cause initially skeptical researchers to reconsider their skepticism.

r002.rationale: The response discusses researchers’ experience with control, planning, and physical systems, but does not attribute their practical expertise to modifying and refining hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think their response is understandable. If you’ve spent years working on control, planning, and modeling, you’re going to ask what machine learning actually adds—and whether it works reliably beyond a demonstration. Those are important questions, especially when a robot interacts with the physical world.

But there’s also a shift in how we approach the problem. Instead of specifying every behavior explicitly, we can let a system learn some of those behaviors from data. That opens up possibilities, particularly for perception and manipulation, where writing down a complete model is difficult.

So I wouldn’t frame it as traditional robotics versus machine learning. The interesting question is how to combine them: where do we want structure and guarantees, and where does learning give us capabilities that are hard to engineer by hand? I think skepticism is productive when it helps us answer that question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses skepticism about what machine learning adds and its reliability, but does not say that demonstrated capabilities may lead traditional robotics researchers to reconsider that skepticism.

r002.rationale: It mentions experience with control, planning, and modeling, but does not attribute practical expertise to extensive experience modifying and refining hardware.
